cases.description: Microsoft's first documented example, at the five decimals it publishes
cases.expected_note: Microsoft publishes =TAN(0.785) = 0.99920 ("Tangent of 0.785 radians"). DERIVATION: tan(0.785) = 0.9992039901050426572858 at 50 digits, which is 0.99920 at the published precision -- 0.9992 as a number, the trailing zero being the page's formatting. Microsoft's page was read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/tan-function. FETCH NOTE FOR THIS BATCH: batch F recorded every /en-us/office/<name>-function-<guid> URL returning Microsoft's 'Sorry, the page you're looking for can't be found' body; today BOTH paths serve the article again -- the GUID form redirects to /en-us/excel/functions/<slug>-function -- and every page cited in this batch came back complete (217-223 KB) in one or two attempts, with no 87 KB stub responses. Nothing here is sourced from a search snippet or a mirror.

cases.description: Microsoft's second documented row: 45 degrees converted by hand
cases.expected_note: Microsoft publishes =TAN(45*PI()/180) = 1. tan(pi/4) = 1 exactly in real arithmetic; the ROUND(...,10) wrapper absorbs the double-precision residue from PI()/180 the same way the SIN(PI()) case does.

cases.description: Microsoft's third documented row: the same angle via RADIANS()
cases.expected_note: Microsoft publishes =TAN(RADIANS(45)) = 1, matching the hand-converted row. Kept separate because it asserts RADIANS() and *PI()/180 agree, which is a different claim from TAN being right.

cases.description: The first example carried to ten decimals
cases.expected_note: Asserted at ten places from the derivation: 0.9992039901. Five published decimals cannot separate tan(0.785) from the nearby exact 1 at tan(pi/4), and pi/4 = 0.7853981634 is only 0.0004 away.

cases.description: tan checked against sin/cos as the engine itself computes them
cases.expected_note: tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) by definition. Asserting the difference is zero makes the engine check TAN against its own SIN and COS, with no constant from us. The TAN page publishes no error-condition remarks at all -- only the degrees-to-radians note -- so no error case is asserted for this function.
